sections: The memory supply–demand gap isn't a single number — it's four different metrics that differ by a factor of 20. Once you standardize on the 'level of adequacy' basis, DRAM and NAND diverge sharply starting in 2027: on a probability-weighted basis, DRAM's growth-rate gap is −6.2% and doesn't close within three years, while NAND turns positive at +6.8% and moves into oversupply by 2028. The divergence between the two reaches 17.4 percentage points on a median basis. The cause has nothing to do with demand — it's entirely in the structure of the two supply equations: NAND has two bit-growth levers that don't require new fabs, and DRAM has none.
Core logic and latest industry developments

1. Two supply equations, and everything starts here. Effective DRAM bits = wafer starts × good die per wafer × bits per die × yield × (1 − HBM wafer penalty). In growth-rate form: bit growth = (1 + wafer capacity growth) × (1 + process-node bit-density gain) × (1 − HBM crowd-out) − 1. Effective NAND bits = wafer starts × die per wafer × layer count × bits per cell × yield. In growth-rate form: bit growth = (1 + wafer capacity growth) × (1 + layer-count gain) × (1 + QLC share gain) − 1.
  2. The entire difference lies in this one line. NAND has two levers that don't require new fabs — going from 232 layers to 400+ layers is +72%, and converting TLC to QLC is +33%; compounded, that's theoretically 2.29x. DRAM has neither. The same demand hits two supply curves with completely different structures, and every conclusion that follows is derived from this one fact.
  3. What the market calls the 'memory gap' actually refers to at least four different things, and their values differ by up to 20x — conflating them is the root of most misreadings. The first layer is the 'notional gap': the amount customers want to buy but can't get, calculated using an allocation method. In 2026 this is −30% or worse — Micron can only fill 50% to two-thirds of demand from key customers, so buyers receive 60% to 70% of what they order. But this layer has a known distortion: customers know they'll be allocated less than they ask for, so they systematically over-order. The second layer is the 'stock gap' — the cumulative level gap under an unconstrained-demand assumption, −15.6% in 2026. This is the model's primary basis. The third layer is the 'clearing gap' — the residual gap in actual transactions after price increases have crowded out some demand. TrendForce's published 'adequacy ratio' is this layer, and it's only −1% to −2% in 2026. The fourth layer is the 'flow gap' — the year-over-year rate of change in the gap, i.e., the first derivative of the second layer, −9.3% in 2026. This is the model's secondary basis.
  4. The logical chain between the four layers runs like this: a notional gap of −30% to −40%, once you strip out customer over-ordering, becomes a stock gap of −15% to −16%; strip out consumer-electronics demand crowded out by price increases (smartphone spec downgrades of −15% to −20%, laptops −14.8%), and it becomes a clearing gap of −1% to −2%. The fourth layer isn't on this chain — it's the first derivative of the second layer.
  5. Inventory is the only physical anchor for the stock-basis gap, and it's the single data point that rewrote the conclusion in v4.0. It stood at 31 weeks in early 2023 — the peak of oversupply, a legacy of double-ordering in 2020–2022. By the end of Q3 2025 it had fallen to 3.3 weeks, on par with the 2018 supercycle trough, with SK Hynix and Micron each at around 2 weeks. Korean media reported in November 2025 that SK Hynix's DRAM inventory had fallen to 2 weeks. It rose back to 4 weeks in July 2026 (taking the midpoint of a 3-to-5-week range), then fell to 1.43 weeks in Q3 2026 — under 10 days. For reference, the industry's 'healthy' level is 30 to 45 days, or 4.3 to 6.4 weeks; the model's assumed 'normal' value is 8 weeks (the industry's long-run average). This 8-week figure is the single most fragile parameter in the entire model, because it simultaneously anchors the starting-point calibration and the restocking-demand assumption.
  6. This is the entire crux of v4.0. For three years the market has been short of supply but has never actually run out, because it's been eating into inventory — drawing down from 31 weeks to under 1.5 weeks, a cumulative destocking of 27.7 weeks over three years, equal to 53% of a full year's demand. That buffer is now gone. The last leg of this drawdown — the 2.57 weeks between July 2026 and Q3 2026 — means about 4.9% of 2026's shipped bits came out of inventory rather than out of production (2.57 divided by 52 equals 4.94%). That volume sits inside the 2026 base, and there's no second round of it in 2027. The entirety of v4.0 turns on this one number.
  7. For DRAM I modeled five scenarios across three years, with probabilities I assigned myself: severe tightness 16%, base case 40%, easing 27%, oversupply 17%, collapse 0%. Take the 40%-probability base case: in 2026, wafer capacity +7%, process-node bit gain +13%, HBM wafer share 22% (top-three-vendor basis), giving supply bit growth of +18.5% against demand growth of 28%, a growth-rate gap of −10.5%. In 2027: wafer +10%, process +12%, HBM share 30%, supply +17.5%, demand 26%, gap −9.5%. In 2028: wafer +16%, process +11%, HBM share 32%, supply +27.3%, demand 24%, gap turns positive to +2.3%.
  8. Breaking down supply growth into three exact factor contributions (the three add up precisely to the total) shows which year carries the heaviest HBM penalty. In 2026: wafer contributes +7.0%, process +13.9%, HBM drag −2.4%, total +18.5% — a figure that has external cross-validation, with IDC at +16% and Micron itself saying 'low-to-mid 20s%'; the model sits between the two. In 2027: wafer +10.0%, process +13.2%, HBM drag −5.7%, total +17.5% — the HBM drag is heaviest in this year. In 2028: wafer +16.0%, process +12.8%, HBM drag −1.5%, total +27.3% — 46% of the three-year capacity addition lands in this single year.
  9. The HBM penalty is the only deduction on the DRAM supply side. The penalty multiplier used for 2025–2026 is 3.0x — both TrendForce and Micron use a 3-to-1 ratio, and KB Securities independently confirmed that HBM4 consumes three times the capacity of conventional DRAM. Starting in 2027, v4.0 lowers this to 2.8x.
  10. DRAM's probability-weighted results: on a flow basis (growth-rate gap), 2026 is −9.6%, 2027 is −4.6%, 2028 is +9.2%, with the trough in 2026. On a stock basis (level of adequacy), the 2025 starting point is −7.0%, 2026 is −14.0%, 2027 is −16.8%, 2028 is −9.4%, with the trough in 2027 — the gap doesn't close within three years.
  11. But the distribution is heavily right-skewed, which makes the mean misleading — the median is the better read on the 'most likely case.' Ranking the five scenarios from most severe to least severe, cumulative probability crosses 50% already within the base case itself — so the probability-weighted mean gets pulled up by the collapse scenario, and the median is the more accurate figure. On a median basis, DRAM's stock gap is −14.6% in 2026, −21.0% in 2027, and −19.5% in 2028 — the gap fails to close in all three years.
  12. The single-variable sensitivity table for 2027 is the single most important table in the whole model, because it proves every supply-side path is blocked. Wafer capacity growth has a base case of 10%, with each percentage point moving the gap by 1.07%; to flip 2027 positive on this lever alone would require adding 8.9 percentage points to reach 20% — physically impossible, since new fabs can't be built that fast: Samsung's P5 doesn't reach mass production until the second half of 2028, and Micron's ID1 doesn't produce first wafers until mid-2027. Process-node bit-density gain has a base case of 12%, with an elasticity of 1.05; it would need to add 9.0 percentage points — equally impossible, since DRAM density has only roughly doubled over a decade, a hard physical wall. HBM wafer share has a base case of 24.6%, with an elasticity of −0.90; it would need to fall by 10.6 percentage points to about 19% — directionally possible, but the magnitude is too large. Demand growth has a base case of 26% to 27%, with an elasticity of −1.00; it would need to fall by 9.5 percentage points to around 15.5% — this is the only realistic path.
  13. So the key takeaway from this table is: all four variables have almost identical unit elasticity (roughly one percentage point of gap movement per one percentage point of variable movement), but their feasible ranges are completely different. All three supply-side paths are physically blocked, so a 2027 flip from shortage to oversupply can only come from the demand side. This is why hyperscaler capex guidance carries more information than any supply-side report. My own caveat: there's a small inconsistency worth flagging here — the sensitivity table uses a 27% demand base case, while the main table's base scenario uses 26%, a 1-point gap. That means '−9.5 points to 15.5%' doesn't quite reconcile with '26% minus 9.5 points equals 16.5%.' It doesn't change the direction of the conclusion, but the final version should reconcile the two.
  14. For NAND I used four scenarios: sustained tightness 25%, base case 46%, shift to oversupply 29%, sharp oversupply 0%. Under the base case, 2026 wafer capacity growth is 0%, layer-count gain +15%, QLC share gain +3%, giving supply bit growth of +17.3% against demand of 22%, a gap of −6.7%. In 2027: wafer +4%, layers +18%, QLC +5%, supply +27.6%, demand 20%, gap turns positive to +5.6%. In 2028: wafer +8%, layers +17%, QLC +5%, supply +31.5%, demand 18%, gap +11.5%.
  15. Note that 2026 wafer growth is 0%, yet supply bits still grow 17.3% — the entire year's bit growth comes from layer count and QLC alone, without a single new wafer. This is a capability DRAM simply doesn't have, and the numbers make the case for themselves. The 2027 three-factor breakdown is wafer +3.0%, layer stacking +18.5%, QLC +6.1% — the layer-count factor alone is bigger than DRAM's entire supply growth rate. In the same year, NAND supply growth divided by DRAM supply growth is 0.93x in 2026, 1.58x in 2027, and 1.15x in 2028.
  16. NAND's probability-weighted results: on a flow basis, 2026 is −6.2%, 2027 is +6.8%, 2028 is +12.8% — turning positive in 2027. On a stock basis, the 2025 starting point is −2.5%, 2026 is −7.4%, 2027 is −2.0%, 2028 is +9.4% — the gap closes and flips to oversupply in 2028. NAND's distribution is skewed even more than DRAM's, so again the median is the better read: +5.6% in 2027 and +11.5% in 2028.
  17. The single most important conclusion: DRAM and NAND diverge sharply starting in 2027. In 2026, DRAM's flow gap of −9.6% versus NAND's −6.2% is a 3.4-point divergence; on a stock basis, −14.0% versus −7.4% is a 6.6-point divergence. In 2027, DRAM's flow gap of −4.6% versus NAND's +6.8% widens the divergence to 11.4 points; on a stock basis, −16.8% versus −2.0% is a 14.8-point divergence; on a median basis the divergence is 17.4 points. In 2028, the stock-basis divergence is 18.8 points, and the median-basis divergence is 25.2 points.
  18. Why the divergence? It has nothing to do with demand. Demand drivers overlap heavily — a single AI server needs DRAM, HBM, and enterprise SSDs at the same time. The cause lies in the structure of the supply equations: NAND can multiply its bits by 2.29x through layer stacking alone, with no new fabs required, while both of DRAM's paths (wafers, process node) are physically blocked, and DRAM also has to absorb an HBM penalty on top. This conclusion holds under all three bases — flow, stock, and median — and the divergence doesn't shrink; if anything, it's widest on a median basis. So the statement that 'pure NAND exposure (SanDisk, Kioxia, Western Digital) and DRAM exposure (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) should be priced separately starting in 2027' isn't just rhetoric.
  19. V4.0 makes three corrections, and their relative sizes are counterintuitive. Correction one: 8-high HBM4 lowers the wafer penalty from 3.0x to 2.8x, which loosens the gap, contributing +0.93 points in 2027. Correction two: inventory exhaustion strips the 2026 drawdown out of the 2027 base, which tightens the gap, contributing −4.94 points — the largest of the three. Correction three: the second round of spec downgrades caps unconstrained demand (counting only the technical half of it), which loosens the gap, contributing +2.50 points. With all three applied, 2027 moves from v3.0's −4.65% to −6.16%, a net change of −1.5 points.
  20. The single most important line in v4.0 is the shift in probability. With only the inventory correction applied, the probability that DRAM is still short in 2027 jumps from 56% to 83% — because the 'easing' scenario, which carries 27% probability, flips from +2.3% (turning to oversupply) to −2.6% (still short). With all three corrections applied, the easing scenario comes back to +0.8%, sitting right back on the boundary, and the probability returns to 56%.
  21. A counterintuitive but important contrast: the headline that Nvidia is requiring 8-high HBM4 sounds like a big deal, but it's only worth 1.3 points in the model. An inventory data point that sounds trivial is worth 5 points. How loud a piece of news is has almost no correlation with how much it actually moves the model.
  22. The arithmetic of 8-high itself is worth recording, because both obvious intuitive answers turn out to be wrong. The first effect is base-die dilution: 8-high is 3.70% worse than 12-high, because every stack needs one non-bit-producing base die, spread over 9 dies instead of 13. The second effect is the compounding of bonding yield across layers — per-layer bonding yield y raised to the power of n — and at y equal to 0.975, 8-high carries a +10.7% yield advantage. The two effects offset each other, netting out to +6.6% net wafer efficiency, which lowers the implied penalty from 3.0x to 2.82x. Intuitive answer A says '8 layers means four fewer dies than 12 layers, so it saves wafers'; intuitive answer B says '8-high only has two-thirds the capacity, so it needs more stacks.' Both only capture half the picture.
  23. On NAND, I'm in direct conflict with KB Securities — and it's a difference in direction, not just degree. On September 7, 2026, KB Securities said that 'NAND and DRAM bit demand growth in 2027 will exceed supply growth by more than 10 percentage points, and the 2027 supply gap will exceed 10%.' My base case says +5.6% in 2027, flipping to oversupply. V4.0's response is to add two levers that move toward KB's view: NAND demand +4.0 points in 2027 (enterprise SSD), and supply −3.0 points (NAND inventory at 4 to 5 weeks is tight, but nowhere near as tight as DRAM's 1.43 weeks). After a combined −7.0 points, the probability-weighted figure moves from +6.8% to −0.25% — close to balanced.

• ☐Has supplier inventory returned above 3 weeks? (Currently under 10 days, i.e., 1.43 weeks.)
  • ☐Can an independent read on enterprise SSD bit demand be obtained? (Currently: none — only KB Securities can be cited.)
  • ☐Has actual shipment share of 8-high HBM4/HBM4E exceeded 50%? (Currently: shipments have just begun.)
  • ☐Has Rubin Ultra's actual HBM capacity spec been confirmed at 384GB? (Currently: an assumed value, unconfirmed.)
  • ☐Has CoWoS and advanced-packaging capacity become a harder constraint than DRAM bits? (Currently: unquantified, outside the model's boundary.)
  • ☐Is HBM's share of total DRAM wafers actually below 26% in 2027? (Currently: TrendForce forecasts 30% by end-2027.)
  • ☐Has the 2027 HBM contract price actually settled above +70%? (Currently: TrendForce forecasts +70% to +140%.)

1. Inventory returns above 3 weeks.
  2. An independent enterprise SSD demand read comes in below 20%.
  3. 8-high HBM4 shipment share exceeds 50%.
  4. Rubin Ultra's actual spec comes in significantly below 384GB.
  5. CoWoS does not become a harder constraint than DRAM bits.
  6. HBM wafer share actually comes in below 26% in 2027.
  7. The 2027 HBM contract price fails to reach +70% or above.
What this means for my positioning

1. DRAM and NAND need to be priced separately, and 2027 is the dividing line. This is the single most tradeable conclusion in the entire model — the 2027 divergence between the two is 17.4 points on a median basis and 25.2 points in 2028, and it's robust across all three bases. I'm keeping my DRAM exposure (Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung); my view on pure NAND exposure (SanDisk) needs an independent enterprise SSD demand read before I can confirm it. Until I have that, my bullish call on SanDisk rests on KB Securities' judgment, not my own measurement — I need to be honest about that.
  2. All three supply-side paths are blocked, so all I need to watch is demand. Flipping 2027 positive through wafer capacity, process gains, or HBM share alone would each require a magnitude that's physically impossible. That means my tracking list can shrink substantially: capex guidance from the four major cloud vendors and Nvidia's supply commitments (currently $279 billion) carry more information than any supply-side report. This is consistent with what I wrote in my Micron note — demand growth is the only first-order variable.
  3. The inventory buffer is spent, so the 2027 shortage is a 'real' shortage. Over the past three years, the market has been short but never actually out of stock because it was drawing down 27.7 weeks of inventory — equal to 53% of a full year's demand. With that buffer gone, any 2027 supply-demand imbalance will show up directly as allocation failures and price increases, not as another round of destocking. This raises my confidence in memory stocks' 2027 earnings resilience, and it's the one substantive change in stance from v3.0 to v4.0.
  4. Part of the bottleneck is moving outside the boundary of this model. Maintaining the same capacity with 8-high stacks requires roughly 1.5x the stack count — base dies up 50%, and interposer area up substantially. The bottleneck is shifting partly from 'DRAM bits' to 'advanced packaging,' which sits outside this model. That means relying on this model alone to judge memory stocks will miss a piece of the picture; I need to track CoWoS capacity separately, and I need to revisit my thinking on companies in the advanced-packaging chain.
  5. On Nvidia's spec downgrade, the strongest signal isn't the number itself. Nvidia's reasons for cutting specs include both technical factors (thermals, power, packaging yield) and supply-driven ones (can't get enough supply). That 'can't get enough supply' half is the strongest evidence that the gap is real — more direct than any supplier's statement. When a buyer voluntarily lowers the spec of its own product, it means the shortage has become hard enough to change downstream product definitions. This is a positive confirmation across all my memory exposure.
  6. Price transmission sits entirely outside this model, and it has already been structurally altered by long-term agreements. The model calculates the supply and demand of physical bits, not price. The price ceilings built into long-term agreements — SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) covers about 50% of FY27 bits — mean that even if the physical shortage persists, price upside will be capped. This is something I have to handle separately at the individual-stock level: the gap arithmetic can tell me whether the shortage will continue, but it can't tell me how much money these companies will actually make.
